en: The Hymn of Mental Worship of Śiva ॥
O Śambhu, whatever was improper or ill-spoken by me toward you, may that become auspicious for the sake of peace; O possessor of all blessings, please accept this worship offered however it may be.
How indeed can I meditate upon you, whose divine majesty is so far beyond the path of the intellect?

O Lord, foremost of gods, from what place should your invocation be made? O Master, what kind of seat should be prepared for you here, once you have taken your seat, so that you may be present everywhere? Where is the water for washing the feet offered, or is it for the hands and feet everywhere?
How could there be a ritual rinsing of the mouth for the Blessed One who faces in all directions?
Or how could there be an offering of honey-mixture here for the Enemy of Madhu, who has already manifested his grace?
What need is there for a bath performed with water for him who is eternally pure?
O Lord of the Gods, there is no need even for a garment here for one who is naked;
for all ornaments shine upon every limb in the form of every auspiciousness.
For you, who transcend the castes and stages of life, there is no excellence whatsoever here to be gained by a sacred thread.
O Lord, since your body is fragrant, what is the point of these perfumes?

I worship you, the bestower of the fruit of Puṣkara, with a Puṣkara flower. O Lord of all, by whom have you—who are the root-wealth of the treasure of tranquility—not been fumigated with incense? 7.105–106.1.
How could a lamp with its flame shine before You, who are self-luminous?
O Blessed One, what indeed is food made of nectar to one who is eternally satisfied?
If this betel, repeatedly offered to You, is only for the sake of coloring Your lips.
O Umāpati, may this entire activity of mine become an offering;
with all my faculties, I perform the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) for that Self which is manifold.
O Śambhu, crown of flowers, may this handful of flowers (*sumanobali*) be for you.

O Lord, how could an umbrella, which merely dispels the heat of the sun, or a fly-whisk, which merely removes the fatigue of fanning, flourish before you, the Great Dancer? O Enemy of the Cities, how could there be song before you, the primordial teacher of the science of music? 11–12.
O Lord of All, how could those who hold the *ḍamaru* drum have the power to play it before You? And for one who is limitless, O Sovereign, who could perform the rite of circumambulation around You?
How, then, O Śaṅkara, could there be meat-offerings for You who exist everywhere?
How can the expansion of my speech possibly reach You, who are beyond the range of words?
Salutations to the eternally blissful; salutations to Him whose form is pure consciousness.
Salutations to the one of boundless compassion; salutations to the one of infinite power and splendor.

May he whose crest is the enemy of the lotus (Śiva), whose head is the merit born from the body of Sagara (the Earth), and whose compassion is a goad for the eyes—may he, who is white with brilliance, appear within the path of my vision.
I take refuge in that essence of consciousness, the expert in the task of protecting the world, the savior of the universe.

(17) O mind, this [essence] has been swallowed by the nectar of his compassion—a nectar that rivals the beauty of blue lotuses, whose half-bodies are shielded by the peaks of the principal mountains, and which is far removed from all impurity. (18)
Salutations to the Lord who possesses a garment made of the sky, whose mountain peak is colored by the clouds,

who possesses a bracelet in the form of the serpent Śeṣa, and who is the half-body of His Consort. Salutations to Him whose eyes remain ever-watchful, causing the lotus to wake and the water-lily to sleep.
I do not know even once [the meaning] beyond Mañjīra, the commentator; how much less, therefore, the end.

(20) We are the servants of the splendors of the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose hair-knots are as red as trumpet-flowers, whose necks possess a dark-blue luster, and whose bodies are pale white—[we who serve] from the boundary of the quarters up to the abode of Brahmā. (21)
In the splendor of the lotus-feet of the Son of the Sage—which bestow longevity upon those whose pride has been robbed by the loss of their memory;

which possess glances thick with a flood of compassion that brings delight to my mind; which are the source of bliss for the worlds and the playful jests of Girijā; and which are the ripening of a heart full of love—[may there be grace]. (22)
May my devotion arise toward that Brahman, whose act of protection is ever-bowing.

(23) At some time or other, may there be before me some indescribable Being, who has shaken off the dark clouds with the shadow of his neck, and whose wife has blossoming brows upon half of his body. (24)

May my mental salutation be offered to the matted locks on the crown of his head, which are dark as rain clouds; to the expanse of his neck, which is blue like a water-bearing cloud; and to his entire white body, which is the very embodiment of light.
(25) [Salutations] to those who shine with the moon, adorned with deer, bulls, and horses, and who bear the Gaṅgā upon their crests.
Enough with others who consider themselves gods of the world but have not overcome the power of passion!

To whom shall I speak of my condition? Who possesses such a heart or such power as this? O Ocean of Compassion, who else has the strength to lift me up from this suffering, were it not for you? (26–27)
O you who are adorned with the crescent moon, I beg of you, who are beyond all novelty: grant me even a small thing; O Blessed One, give me my very own nature, which is bliss.
O Blessed One, whether through childishness, or through devotion, or through being overwhelmed by calamity—

Or, whatever harsh words have been uttered by me in my mind due to being possessed by delusion— [forgive them]. O Great Lord, whether it be Your supremacy over the universe, the true meaning of the Vedas, Agamas, and Purāṇas,
or Your compassion toward the undevoted, [grant this] here, You whose desires are already fulfilled.
Thus ends the hymn of mental worship of Śiva composed by Śivānanda Avadhūta.
